title: I keep seeing people say Three.js is only good for prototypes, so I built this
author: ledniv
selftext:
I have seen several posts claiming that Three.js is fine for prototypes, but not for high-performance games.

I don’t think Three.js is necessarily the problem. The way a game’s data is organized and processed has a huge effect on performance, regardless of which renderer you use.

So I created **Swarm** with Astra as a demonstration:

[https://swarm.nitzan.games/](https://swarm.nitzan.games/)

The goal was to process and render a large number of entities using JavaScript and Three.js, but with a data-oriented architecture.

A typical implementation might create a separate JavaScript object for every entity. Each object owns its position, velocity, health, references, update method, and Three.js object. At scale, this can mean scattered data, more garbage collection, a large scene graph, and far too many draw calls.

Swarm takes a different approach.

Frequently processed state is stored in typed arrays:

    const x  = new Float32Array(MAX_ENTITIES);
    const y  = new Float32Array(MAX_ENTITIES);
    const vx = new Float32Array(MAX_ENTITIES);
    const vy = new Float32Array(MAX_ENTITIES);
    
    for (let i = 0; i < entityCount; i++) {
        x[i] += vx[i] * dt;
        y[i] += vy[i] * dt;
    }

Typed arrays store fixed-width values in contiguous memory. Processing them sequentially gives the CPU predictable access patterns and better data locality. When a cache line is loaded, it contains several of the values the loop is about to process.

The architecture also:

* Uses array indices as entity IDs.
* Preallocates memory and reuses inactive slots.
* Avoids allocations during the frame loop.
* Processes movement, collision, damage, and other behavior in centralized loops.
* Keeps the simulation data separate from the Three.js presentation.

The demo now lets you render the swarm using either simple shapes or 3D models. The underlying simulation does not need to change because it is independent of the presentation. The same arrays and systems drive both visual options.

Rendering still needs attention. Creating thousands of independent meshes and draw calls will be expensive. When objects share geometry and materials, Three.js provides tools such as `InstancedMesh` to render them together. The simulation arrays remain the source of truth, while the rendering layer displays their current state.

This addresses both sides of the problem: cache-friendly simulation and batched rendering.

Three.js is a rendering library rather than a complete game engine, but that is very different from saying it is only useful for prototypes. You can build high-performance games with it if the architecture is designed for the amount of data being processed.

I gave Astra my reusable data-oriented design skill so it would follow these rules while building the demo:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Try both visual modes and let me know how they perform in your browser. I’m also curious what limitations people have run into with Three.js that led them to conclude it was only suitable for prototyping.

replies.author: ledniv
replies.body:
Prototype, as in something that needs to be rebuilt in a real game engine to turn into a full game. 

This shows three.js can do high performance just as well as other game engines.

replies.author: freqCake
replies.body: A prototype is something you build to learn something from

comments.body: Great prototype. Are you going to turn it into a game?

comments.author: thygrrr
comments.body: Dude, this is literally a prototype that answers the question whether you can run high perf in three.js (which was already known). It's also bespoke code so it's not even an tech demo :)
